Chapter 9. The Shadow of the Crash—Legacy in a Time of Crisis.
Imagine this: just months after Calvin Coolidge left the White House, the nation was thrown into chaos. The stock market crashed, banks crumbled, and suddenly, millions of Americans found themselves out of work. That sense of prosperity everyone felt during the roaring twenties? It disappeared almost overnight, replaced by fear and uncertainty.
In the wake of the Great Depression, Coolidge’s legacy became a hot topic. Some folks pointed the finger at him, saying his focus on limited government made the country more fragile. But others stepped up to defend him, reminding everyone that the causes of the Depression were tangled and complicated—and honestly, who could’ve predicted a disaster on that scale?
Coolidge watched all this unfold with a heavy heart. Deep down, he still believed in the values he’d always stood for: thrift, honesty, and restraint. Even as times got tough, he worried the country might abandon those ideals in search of quick fixes and simple solutions. Every now and then, he spoke out—reminding people to be patient, to persevere—but he understood that the world had changed in ways no one expected.
For many, the memory of Coolidge’s years in office became almost like a touchstone. It was a reminder of a time when government was smaller, taxes were lower, and the economy seemed unstoppable. Some saw him as a symbol of lost stability, while others criticized him for not seeing the dangers that lay ahead. And that debate about his legacy? It didn’t fade away—it kept evolving, shaped by the shifting tides of history.
Most people don’t realize just how tricky it is to judge a leader’s choices in hindsight. Coolidge made his decisions based on the world he lived in, and the values he believed in most. To him, freedom and responsibility were two sides of the same coin. And at the end of the day, he trusted the American people—believing that was the best way he could serve his country.
